description: Reading and writing data, working with the file system, and interacting with the operating system. Import and Export handle several hundred file formats with automatic detection; the lower-level stream functions give byte- and line-level control; and the process functions run external programs and read their output.

tools.name: Print
tools.description: Prints expressions to the standard output, concatenating its arguments side by side and adding a newline. In a notebook the output appears as a print cell; under wolframscript it goes to stdout, which makes it the basic logging primitive for scripts. Print returns Null, so it never contributes a value to the surrounding expression.
tools.example:
Print["Result: ", 42]
Print["x = ", x, ", y = ", y]
Do[Print[i^2], {i, 3}]
Print[Style["warning", Red]]
tools.notes: Print output is not capturable as a value; use Echo to print and return, or WriteString[$Output, ...] for output without a newline.

tools.name: Echo
tools.description: Prints an expression and returns it unchanged, which makes it a drop-in debugging probe that can be inserted anywhere in a pipeline. Echo[expr, label] prefixes a label and Echo[expr, label, f] prints f[expr] while still returning the original value. EchoFunction is the operator form for use inside composition chains.
tools.usage:
Echo[expr]
Echo[expr, label]
Echo[expr, label, f]
EchoFunction[f][expr]
tools.example:
2 + Echo[3 * 4]
Echo[Range[10], "data: ", Length]
Total[Echo /@ {1, 2, 3}]
Range[5] // EchoFunction[Total] // Mean
tools.notes: Because Echo returns its argument, you can insert and remove it without restructuring code, unlike Print.

tools.name: Import
tools.description: Reads a file, URL or cloud object and converts it into a Wolfram Language expression, detecting the format from the extension or content. An explicit format string overrides detection, and an element specification selects a particular part such as "Data", "Rows", "Plaintext" or a named sheet. Several hundred formats are supported including CSV, JSON, XLSX, XML, HDF5, images, audio, PDF and archives.
tools.usage:
Import["file"]
Import["file", "format"]
Import["file", elements]
Import["file", {"format", element}]
Import["url"]

parameters.name: elements
parameters.description: Which part to return, e.g. "Data", "Elements", "Rows", {"Data", 1} for the first sheet.

parameters.name: HeaderLines
parameters.description: Number of leading lines to treat as headers for tabular formats.

tools.example:
Import["data.csv"]
Import["data.csv", "Dataset", HeaderLines -> 1]
Import["config.json"]
Import["book.xlsx", {"Data", 1}]
Import["https://example.com/data.json", "RawJSON"]
Import["file.xlsx", "Elements"]
tools.notes: Import["file", "Elements"] lists what can be extracted from a given file, which is the quickest way to discover the right element name. Use SemanticImport when you want types (dates, quantities, entities) inferred automatically.

tools.name: Export
tools.description: Writes a Wolfram Language expression to a file in a chosen format, inferring the format from the file extension when it is not given explicitly. It handles data tables, graphics, notebooks, audio, video, 3D geometry and archives, and returns the file name on success. Format-specific options control compression, image resolution and delimiters.
tools.usage:
Export["file", expr]
Export["file", expr, "format"]
Export["file", expr, elements]
Export["file", expr, opts]
tools.example:
Export["out.csv", {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Export["plot.png", Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}], ImageResolution -> 300]
Export["data.json", <|"a" -> 1, "b" -> {1, 2}|>]
Export["model.wxf", expr, "WXF"]
Export["table.xlsx", Table[{i, i^2}, {i, 10}]]
tools.notes: Exporting graphics to PNG or JPEG rasterizes at ImageResolution dpi; use PDF or SVG for vector output that scales cleanly.

tools.name: ImportString
tools.description: Parses a string as if it were the contents of a file in a given format, without touching the file system. It is the right function for data received over a network, embedded in a script or produced by another process. Unlike Import it usually requires an explicit format because there is no extension to infer from.
tools.example:
ImportString["1,2\n3,4", "CSV"]
ImportString["{\"a\": 1}", "RawJSON"]
ImportString["a b c", "Table"]
ImportString[response, "JSON"]
tools.notes: "RawJSON" produces Associations while "JSON" produces lists of rules; RawJSON is usually the more convenient form.

tools.name: ExportString
tools.description: Serializes an expression into a string in a chosen format, instead of writing it to a file. It is used to build HTTP request bodies, to embed data in generated text and to inspect exactly what Export would write. For binary formats use ExportByteArray, which returns a ByteArray rather than a string.
tools.example:
ExportString[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, "CSV"]
ExportString[<|"a" -> 1|>, "RawJSON"]
ExportString[Plot[Sin[x], {x, 0, Pi}], "SVG"] // Short
ExportByteArray[img, "PNG"]

tools.name: Put
tools.description: Writes an expression to a file in InputForm, replacing any existing contents, and is written in shorthand as expr >> "file". The file can later be read back with Get. PutAppend (>>>) adds to the end of an existing file instead.
tools.example:
{1, 2, 3} >> "data.wl"
Put[x^2 + 1, "expr.wl"]
Get["data.wl"]
Put[<|"a" -> 1|>, "config.wl"]
tools.notes: Put writes human-readable text that round-trips exactly; DumpSave writes a much faster binary form that is version-specific.

tools.name: PutAppend
tools.description: Appends an expression in InputForm to the end of a file, written in shorthand as expr >>> "file". Reading such a file with Get evaluates each expression in turn, so it works as a simple append-only log of results. It creates the file if it does not exist.
tools.example:
1 >>> "log.wl"
2 >>> "log.wl"
ReadList["log.wl"]
Do[PutAppend[{i, i^2}, "results.wl"], {i, 5}]

tools.name: Save
tools.description: Writes the complete definitions of symbols to a file in readable InputForm, including down values, attributes and options, appending rather than overwriting. Reloading the file with Get recreates the definitions exactly. It is the simple way to persist a function or a computed table between sessions.
tools.notes: Save follows dependencies on other symbols mentioned in the definitions, so the output file can be larger than expected.

tools.name: DumpSave
tools.description: Writes symbol definitions to a binary .mx file that loads far faster than re-parsing source, because the expressions are stored in the kernel's internal format. The file is specific to the Wolfram Language version and the machine architecture, so it is a cache rather than a distribution format. Load it back with Get like any other file.
tools.notes: Never distribute .mx files as the only copy of your code: they cannot be read by a different kernel version and are not human-readable.

tools.name: OpenRead
tools.description: Opens a file or URL as an input stream so it can be read incrementally with Read, ReadLine or ReadString. It returns an InputStream object used as the handle for subsequent reads, and the stream must be closed with Close. Use it for files too large to import at once, or when you need to stop reading partway through.
tools.notes: Always Close the stream, ideally inside a try/finally structure, or the file handle stays open for the session.

tools.name: OpenWrite
tools.description: Opens a file as an output stream for writing, truncating any existing contents; OpenAppend opens for appending instead. Write, WriteString and WriteLine then send data to the returned OutputStream object. This is the efficient pattern for generating a large file incrementally rather than building the whole content in memory.

tools.name: Read
tools.description: Reads one object of a specified type from an input stream, advancing the stream position. Types include Number, Real, Integer, Word, String, Record, Byte and Expression, and a list of types reads several objects into a list. It returns EndOfFile when the stream is exhausted.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Byte, Character, Expression, Number, Real, Integer, Record, String or Word.

parameters.name: RecordSeparators
parameters.description: Strings that delimit Record objects, default newline.

tools.example:
str = StringToStream["1 2 3"];
Read[str, Number]
Read[str, {Number, Number}]
Close[str]
str = OpenRead["data.txt"]; Read[str, String]

tools.name: ReadList
tools.description: Reads a whole file or stream into a list of objects of a given type, which is the quickest way to slurp structured text. ReadList["file", Number] gives all the numbers and ReadList["file", String] gives all the lines. Options such as RecordSeparators and WordSeparators customize the parsing.
tools.usage:
ReadList["file"]
ReadList["file", type]
ReadList["file", type, n]
ReadList[stream, {t1, t2}]
tools.example:
ReadList["numbers.txt", Number]
ReadList["data.txt", String]
ReadList["table.txt", {Number, Number}]
ReadList["file.csv", String, 10]
ReadList[StringToStream["1 2 3"], Number]
tools.notes: For well-known tabular formats Import is usually simpler and faster; ReadList is best for irregular text where you need explicit control.

tools.name: ReadLine
tools.description: Reads one line of text from a stream, returning it as a string without the newline, or EndOfFile at the end. It is the standard building block of a line-by-line processing loop over a large file. Combined with a While loop it keeps memory use constant regardless of file size.

tools.name: ReadString
tools.description: Reads the entire remaining contents of a file or stream as a single string, or up to a given terminator. ReadString["file"] is the simplest way to slurp a whole text file. It also works on process streams and URLs.
tools.usage:
ReadString["file"]
ReadString[stream]
ReadString[stream, terminator]
ReadString[stream, n]
tools.example:
ReadString["notes.txt"]
StringLength[ReadString["big.txt"]]
str = OpenRead["data.txt"];
ReadString[str, "\n"]
ReadString["file.txt", 100]

tools.name: Write
tools.description: Writes expressions to an output stream in InputForm followed by a newline, so the result can be read back with Read or Get. Several expressions in one call are written separated by spaces. It is the structured counterpart of WriteString, which writes raw text.

tools.name: WriteString
tools.description: Writes strings to a stream exactly as given, with no newline and no quoting, converting non-string arguments with a text form. It is the function for producing precisely formatted output files and for printing without a line break. WriteString[$Output, ...] writes to the console.
tools.usage:
WriteString[stream, str1, str2, ...]
WriteString["file", str]
WriteString[$Output, str]
tools.notes: Non-string arguments are converted using OutputForm, which can reformat numbers; call ToString[x, InputForm] first when exact text matters.

tools.name: WriteLine
tools.description: Writes a string to a stream followed by a newline, which is the common case when producing line-oriented output. It is a convenience wrapper over WriteString and works with file streams, process streams and $Output. Use it for log files and for feeding stdin of an external process.

tools.name: Close
tools.description: Closes an open input or output stream, flushing any buffered output and releasing the file handle. It accepts a stream object or a file name. Failing to close an output stream can leave data unwritten and the file locked on Windows.

tools.name: Streams
tools.description: Lists the currently open streams, including the standard $Output and $Messages channels. It is the way to find and close streams that were left open by an interrupted computation. A name pattern filters the list to streams for a particular file.
tools.example:
Streams[]
Streams["out.txt"]
Length[Streams[]]
Close /@ Streams["tmp.txt"]

tools.name: FileNames
tools.description: Lists files and directories matching a name pattern, optionally searching a list of directories to a specified depth. FileNames["*.csv", dir, Infinity] performs a recursive search. Patterns use shell-style wildcards or full string patterns, and results are returned as full paths.
tools.usage:
FileNames[]
FileNames["pattern"]
FileNames["pattern", {dirs}]
FileNames["pattern", dir, levels]
tools.example:
FileNames["*.wl"]
FileNames["*.csv", "C:\\data"]
FileNames["*.txt", NotebookDirectory[], Infinity]
FileNames["*", $HomeDirectory, 1]
Length[FileNames["*.png", dir, Infinity]]
tools.notes: FileNames is case-insensitive on Windows and macOS but case-sensitive on Linux; use IgnoreCase -> True for portable behaviour.

tools.name: FileExistsQ
tools.description: Tests whether a file or directory exists at the given path, returning True or False without raising errors. It is the standard guard before Import or DeleteFile. Related predicates include DirectoryQ, FileByteCount, FileDate and FileHash.
tools.example:
FileExistsQ["data.csv"]
If[FileExistsQ[path], Import[path], {}]
FileExistsQ[FileNameJoin[{dir, "out.txt"}]]
FileByteCount["data.csv"]

tools.name: DirectoryQ
tools.description: Tests whether a path refers to an existing directory rather than a file. It is used to separate directories from files in FileNames output and to decide whether to recurse. Directory listings can then be filtered with Select[FileNames[...], DirectoryQ].
tools.example:
DirectoryQ[$HomeDirectory]
DirectoryQ["data.csv"]
Select[FileNames["*", dir], DirectoryQ]
If[!DirectoryQ[out], CreateDirectory[out]]

tools.name: CreateDirectory
tools.description: Creates a new directory, with CreateIntermediateDirectories -> True making all missing parent directories as well. Called with no argument it creates a uniquely named temporary directory and returns its path. It returns the path on success and issues a message if the directory already exists.
tools.example:
CreateDirectory["output"]
CreateDirectory[FileNameJoin[{base, "run1", "logs"}], CreateIntermediateDirectories -> True]
tmp = CreateDirectory[];
DeleteDirectory[tmp]

tools.name: DeleteFile
tools.description: Permanently deletes one or more files, returning Null on success and issuing a message if a file cannot be removed. DeleteDirectory removes directories, with DeleteContents -> True to remove non-empty ones. There is no undo, so guard with FileExistsQ and be careful with wildcards.
tools.usage:
DeleteFile["file"]
DeleteFile[{f1, f2, ...}]
DeleteDirectory["dir", DeleteContents -> True]
tools.example:
DeleteFile["tmp.txt"]
DeleteFile[FileNames["*.tmp", workDir]]
DeleteDirectory[tempDir, DeleteContents -> True]
If[FileExistsQ[f], DeleteFile[f]]

tools.name: CopyFile
tools.description: Copies a file to a new location, returning the new path. By default it refuses to overwrite an existing target unless OverwriteTarget -> True is given. CopyDirectory does the same for whole directory trees.
tools.usage:
CopyFile["source", "target"]
CopyFile[src, dst, OverwriteTarget -> True]
CopyDirectory["src", "dst"]
tools.example:
CopyFile["data.csv", "backup/data.csv"]
CopyFile[src, dst, OverwriteTarget -> True]
CopyDirectory["project", "project_backup"]

tools.name: RenameFile
tools.description: Renames or moves a file, returning the new path. Like CopyFile it will not overwrite an existing target unless OverwriteTarget -> True is set. RenameDirectory performs the same operation on directories.
tools.usage:
RenameFile["old", "new"]
RenameFile[old, new, OverwriteTarget -> True]
RenameDirectory["old", "new"]
tools.example:
RenameFile["draft.txt", "final.txt"]
RenameFile[tmpOut, finalOut, OverwriteTarget -> True]
RenameDirectory["v1", "v2"]
tools.notes: Renaming across filesystems or drives may fail; copy then delete in that case.

tools.name: FileNameJoin
tools.description: Joins path components with the correct separator for the current operating system, producing a portable path. FileNameSplit is the inverse, breaking a path into its components. Always use these instead of string concatenation with slashes, which breaks between platforms.
tools.example:
FileNameJoin[{$HomeDirectory, "data", "in.csv"}]
FileNameSplit["C:\\data\\in.csv"]
FileNameJoin[{NotebookDirectory[], "results", "out.json"}]
FileNameJoin[{"a", "b"}, OperatingSystem -> "Unix"]

tools.name: FileBaseName
tools.description: Gives the name of a file without its directory path or its extension, with FileExtension giving the extension alone and FileNameTake giving the last component including the extension. FileNameDrop removes leading path components. Together they cover all the usual path-manipulation needs.
tools.example:
FileBaseName["C:\\data\\report.csv"]
FileExtension["report.csv"]
FileNameTake["C:\\data\\report.csv"]
FileNameDrop["C:\\data\\report.csv", -1]
FileBaseName[#] <> ".json" & /@ files

tools.name: SetDirectory
tools.description: Changes the current working directory and pushes the previous one onto a stack, which ResetDirectory pops. Directory[] gives the current working directory. Relative paths in Import, Export and OpenRead are resolved against it.
tools.example:
Directory[]
SetDirectory["C:\\projects\\analysis"];
FileNames[]
ResetDirectory[]
SetDirectory[NotebookDirectory[]]
tools.notes: Prefer absolute paths built with FileNameJoin over changing the working directory, especially in scripts that may be run from anywhere.

tools.name: $HomeDirectory
tools.description: The user's home directory as a string. Related system directory variables include $UserBaseDirectory (where user packages and preferences live), $InstallationDirectory, $TemporaryDirectory, $InitialDirectory and $BaseDirectory. They give portable anchors for building paths.
tools.example:
$HomeDirectory
$UserBaseDirectory
FileNameJoin[{$HomeDirectory, "Documents", "data.csv"}]
$TemporaryDirectory
$InstallationDirectory

tools.name: NotebookDirectory
tools.description: Gives the directory containing the current notebook, which is the usual anchor for relative data paths in interactive work. It requires the notebook to have been saved and only works when a front end is present. In a wolframscript run use DirectoryName[$InputFileName] instead.
tools.example:
NotebookDirectory[]
SetDirectory[NotebookDirectory[]]
Import[FileNameJoin[{NotebookDirectory[], "data.csv"}]]
DirectoryName[$InputFileName]
tools.notes: In a headless script $InputFileName holds the running file's path; NotebookDirectory[] fails without a front end.

tools.name: Run
tools.description: Executes a command in the operating system shell and returns only its exit code; the output goes to the terminal rather than back to the kernel. It is the simplest way to fire off an external command when the output is not needed. Use RunProcess when you need to capture stdout, stderr or the exit code together.
tools.example:
Run["echo hello"]
Run["python script.py"]
Run["mkdir", "newdir"]
If[Run["git status"] != 0, Print["failed"]]
tools.notes: Run does not capture output and is not portable across shells; RunProcess is the recommended modern replacement.

tools.name: RunProcess
tools.description: Runs an external program to completion and returns an Association with "ExitCode", "StandardOutput" and "StandardError". The command is given as a list of the executable and its arguments, avoiding shell quoting problems, and optional arguments supply stdin text, a working directory and environment variables. It is the standard way to call other tools from a Wolfram Language script.
tools.usage:
RunProcess[{"exe", "arg1", ...}]
RunProcess[cmd, "StandardOutput"]
RunProcess[cmd, All, input]
RunProcess[cmd, All, input, ProcessDirectory -> dir]
tools.example:
RunProcess[{"git", "rev-parse", "HEAD"}]
RunProcess[{"python", "-c", "print(2+2)"}, "StandardOutput"]
res = RunProcess[{"ls", "-l"}];
res["ExitCode"]
RunProcess[{"sort"}, "StandardOutput", "b\na\nc\n"]
tools.notes: Passing the command as a list avoids shell interpretation entirely, which is both safer and more portable than a single command string.

tools.name: StartProcess
tools.description: Starts an external program asynchronously and returns a ProcessObject whose stdin, stdout and stderr are ordinary Wolfram Language streams. This lets you interact with a long-running program, feeding it input and reading output incrementally. ProcessStatus, KillProcess and ProcessConnection manage the running process.
tools.usage:
StartProcess[{"exe", args}]
ProcessConnection[proc, "StandardOutput"]
WriteLine[proc, "text"]
ReadLine[proc]
KillProcess[proc]
tools.notes: Remember to kill or close processes you start; orphaned children keep running after the kernel exits on some platforms.

tools.name: Environment
tools.description: Gives the value of an operating system environment variable as a string, or $Failed when it is not set. SetEnvironment changes a variable for the kernel process and its children, and GetEnvironment with no argument returns all of them as rules. These are the usual way to read configuration and secrets in a script.
tools.example:
Environment["PATH"]
Environment["HOME"]
GetEnvironment["USERNAME"]
SetEnvironment["MY_API_KEY" -> "secret"];
Length[GetEnvironment[]]

tools.name: $CommandLine
tools.description: The list of raw command-line arguments with which the kernel was launched, including the executable path and kernel options. For scripts run with wolframscript, $ScriptCommandLine is the more useful variable because it contains only the script name and the arguments intended for it. $ProcessID, $MachineName and $SystemID give other details about the running process.
tools.example:
$CommandLine
$ScriptCommandLine
$SystemID
$MachineName
$ProcessID

tools.name: Pause
tools.description: Suspends evaluation for the given number of seconds, accepting fractional values. It is used to throttle polling loops, to wait for an external process and to pace animations. The kernel remains responsive to abort requests during the pause.
tools.example:
Pause[1]
Do[Print[i]; Pause[0.5], {i, 3}]
While[!FileExistsQ["result.txt"], Pause[2]]
AbsoluteTiming[Pause[0.25]]

tools.name: TimeConstrained
tools.description: Evaluates an expression but aborts it after a specified number of seconds, returning $Aborted or an optional failure expression instead. It is the standard guard around a computation that might not terminate, such as an open-ended Simplify or Solve. MemoryConstrained provides the same protection against runaway memory use.
tools.usage:
TimeConstrained[expr, t]
TimeConstrained[expr, t, failexpr]
MemoryConstrained[expr, b, failexpr]
tools.example:
TimeConstrained[FullSimplify[expr], 10]
TimeConstrained[While[True, Null], 1, "timed out"]
TimeConstrained[Integrate[f, x], 30, NIntegrate[f, {x, 0, 1}]]
MemoryConstrained[Table[i, {i, 10^9}], 10^8, $Failed]
tools.notes: The abort is checked at evaluation boundaries, so a single long-running internal LAPACK or kernel call may overshoot the limit.
